results.summary: This project implements a washing machine controller using a finite-state-machine in Verilog. It simulates a simplified washing process with stages that can be controlled by start and mode select buttons, and a door closed input. The system outputs control signals for a water valve, wash motor, and spin motor, and indicates completion with an LED. Testing involves using buttons and levers to simulate inputs and observing LED outputs.

This is an implementation of a simple 8-bit SUBNEG CPU designed to interface with external parallel SRAM. The CPU requires external hardware for memory addressing and output latching, and programs must be loaded into the SRAM externally before enabling the CPU. Testing involves providing the necessary external components and loading a program into the SRAM. The design is notable for its minimal instruction set and reliance on external memory.

This project is a basic oscilloscope and signal generator implemented in VHDL, utilizing external Pmod modules for ADC, DAC, FRAM, and HDMI output. It captures input signals, buffers them to external FRAM, and displays them on an HDMI screen, albeit rotated due to memory constraints. The signal generator produces basic waveforms, and control is managed via buttons and switches. Testing requires connecting various Pmods and observing the HDMI output, with an optional Python script for processing captured frames.

Fastest Finger is a simple game designed to show which button was pressed first among several inputs. When a button is pressed, if all other buttons are low, the corresponding output is set high. Testing involves connecting buttons to the inputs and observing the LEDs, where the first pressed button's corresponding LED will illuminate. The design is implemented using Wokwi and serves as a basic demonstration of input prioritization.

This analog module provides two multiplexers, one with 4 passgates and another with 8, allowing analog signals to be switched or multiplexed. It includes a ring oscillator for generating a high-frequency clock, a digital block for controlling the passgates, and a counter for driving signals through the multiplexers. Testing involves observing the passgate behavior and chaining the multiplexers, requiring external analog components and a video demonstration for guidance. The design aims to facilitate debugging and inspection of analog projects.

This project implements a 1.2V Brokaw bandgap voltage reference with a PTAT (Proportional To Absolute Temperature) current generator. It uses SKY130 PNP BJTs and an OTA with feedback to produce a stable reference voltage. Testing involves applying 1.8V VDD and measuring the Vref output, with expected values around 1.2-1.3V, and characterizing its stability across a temperature range. No external hardware is required for basic testing.

This project is a simple I2C master controller implemented in Verilog that transmits a single byte to a fixed slave address (0x50). It generates START and STOP conditions and provides BUSY, DONE, and ACK status outputs. Testing involves applying reset, providing an 8-bit data value, asserting START, and observing the SDA and SCL signals. An external I2C slave device or logic analyzer is recommended for observation.

This project wraps a high-speed crystal oscillator (HSXO) IP block into a Tiny Tapeout project using the analog template. It requires external hardware including a passive crystal and load capacitors to form a Pierce oscillator circuit. Testing involves applying a bias current, enabling the oscillator, and observing a clock signal on the DOUT pin. The design is intended for high-speed clock generation, with specific considerations for crystal frequency and trace lengths.

TinySensor uses external hardware photodiodes as inputs to measure light intensity, displaying the total value on a 7-segment display. The design aggregates inputs from photodiodes (or dip switches for testing) and shows the result on the display. It includes clock and reset inputs, and outputs for the 7-segment display segments. Testing involves connecting photodiodes or using dip switches to provide input values and observing the 7-segment output.

This design implements a 6-bit FIFO with 52 entries, featuring a chain of latches for the first 48 entries and a ring of flip-flops for the last 4. It provides access to the oldest four entries via a peek address. The FIFO includes ready and empty status outputs, and its operation is controlled by mode inputs for write enable, reset, pop, and peek address. Testing involves managing these inputs to write, read, and peek at data, with considerations for FIFO fullness affecting write readiness.
